name: The Price of Everything: A Micro-Transaction Satire
author: Jin Park-Oladele — Neural-Feed Satirist
description:
I woke up this morning and checked my balance. It was Φ0.003 less than when I fell asleep, because my BCI processed 14 neural-feed advertisements during REM sleep and charged me Φ0.0002 per impression for the "premium dream-adjacent content integration experience." I didn't ask for premium dream-adjacent content integration. I was dreaming about my dead mother. Sterling-Nakamura's behavioral prediction algorithm determined that my elevated emotional state during the dream made me 34% more susceptible to nostalgia-themed consumer messaging, so it served me ads for memorial hologram services while I cried in my sleep. I was charged for the privilege.

I got out of bed. My atmospheric processor clicked from sleep mode to active mode: Φ0.008 per minute. I breathed. I breathed again. Each breath cost me nothing — per-breath billing was outlawed in 2194, thank the QFIC for their boundless mercy — but the air I breathed cost Φ0.008 per minute regardless of whether I was breathing or holding my breath in protest. I stood in my 18-square-meter hab unit and held my breath for as long as I could. Forty-seven seconds. I saved no money. I felt briefly powerful. Then I breathed and the feeling passed.

I walked to the communal hygiene station. Transit through the corridor: Φ0.001 per 10 meters, billed as "infrastructure maintenance contribution." The hygiene station: Φ0.15 for a 3-minute water allocation, Φ0.02 for soap from the dispenser, Φ0.05 for 2 minutes of heated air drying. Total morning hygiene: Φ0.22. I calculated that I could reduce this to Φ0.07 by eliminating heated drying (air-dry in the corridor), using my own soap (purchased in bulk at Φ0.80 per 500ml, amortized over approximately 60 uses: Φ0.013 per use, saving Φ0.007 per hygiene event), and reducing my water allocation to 2 minutes (Φ0.10). I have become the kind of person who optimizes soap expenditure to the third decimal place. I have a degree in literature. I once wrote a thesis on the use of silence in Chekhov. Now I calculate the cost-per-use of soap. Quanta has made an accountant of everyone. Chekhov would have understood. Chekhov understood everything.

I ate breakfast. A printed protein bar from the block dispenser: Φ0.35. I wanted two. I ate one. I did the math and decided that the second bar's marginal utility did not justify the Φ0.35 expenditure given my projected daily micro-transaction bleed of Φ1.40 and my current balance of Φ18.72 with 11 days until the next UBC deposit. This is what Quanta has done to hunger: it has made it a math problem. My stomach said eat. My BCI said Φ18.72 minus Φ0.35 minus projected daily expenses of Φ4.20 times 11 remaining days equals negative Φ27.83. My stomach lost the argument. My stomach always loses the argument. The numbers are merciless and the numbers are always right and the numbers say that being a little hungry today means being a little less hungry on day 11. I finished my protein bar. It tasted like mathematics. Everything tastes like mathematics now. The food, the air, the water, the dreams. Sterling-Nakamura has priced the world down to the last decimal place and I live in the remainders, in the fractions too small to matter and too numerous to escape. I am Φ18.72 worth of person today. Tomorrow I will be less.
story_hooks: Jin's satirical pieces attract a massive following, and a corponation offers to sponsor them — for a price that would compromise their independence
The atmospheric processing company cited in the piece sues for defamation, revealing that the actual per-minute rates are even higher than Jin described
